title: Facile synthesis of hierarchical flower-like Ag/Cu2O and Au/ Cu2O nanostructures and enhanced catalytic performance in electrochemical reduction of CO2
abstract: Novel, hierarchical, flower-like Ag/Cu2O and Au/Cu2O nanostructures were successfully fabricated and applied as efficient electrocatalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2. Cu2O nanospheres with a uniform size of ~180 nm were initially synthesized. Thereafter, Cu2O was used as a sacrificial template to prepare a series of Ag/Cu2O composites through galvanic replacement. By varying the Ag/Cu atomic ratio, Ag0.125/Cu2O, having a hierarchical, flower-like nanostructure with intersecting Ag nanoflakes encompassing an inner Cu2O sphere, was prepared. The as-prepared Agx/Cu2O samples presented higher Faradaic efficiencies (FE) for CO and relatively suppressed H2 evolution than the parent Cu2O nanospheres due to the combination of Ag with Cu2O in the former. Notably, the highest CO evolution rate was achieved with Ag0.125/Cu2O due to the larger electroactive surface area furnished by the hierarchical structure. The same hierarchical flower-like structure was also obtained for the Au0.6/Cu2O composite, where the FECO (10%) was even higher than that of Ag0.125/Cu2O. Importantly, the results reveal that Ag0.125/Cu2O and Au0.6/Cu2O both exhibit remarkably improved stability relative to Cu2O. This study presents a facile method of developing hierarchical metaloxide composites as efficient and stable electrocatalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2.

sections.text: Keywords bimetallic nanostructure, hierarchical metal/ oxide nanomaterial, galvanic replacement, electrochemical reduction of CO2

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Bimetallic nanostructured materials are an attractive class of nanomaterials for application in the fields of catalysis, sensing, and optics [1–4]. Recently, metal/oxide bimetallic nanostructures consisting of one zero-valent metal and the other in an oxidized state have drawn even more interest due to the combination of the favorable catalytic properties of the metal and metal oxides [5,6]. Among the various strategies for constructing metal/oxide bimetallic systems, galvanic replacement stands out as an efficient and facile approach. Generally, oxides in low oxidation states, such as Cu2O and Co3O4, are used as sacrificial templates to generate more diversified and complex materials [7,8]. Cu2O is often utilized because of its susceptibility to oxidation and dissolution by many other species under appropriate conditions. However, the primary advantage is that the composition and structure of the formed metal/ oxide system can be controlled by adjusting the metal precursor-to-metal oxide ratio, while the shape and particle size distribution can be tailored by employing metal oxides with different geometries as the templates [9–12]. Therefore, galvanic replacement is a potentially superior strategy for fabricating diverse metal/oxide materials to achieve efficient electrocatalytic performance. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ERC) to generate valuable liquid fuels or chemicals is a very promising method of addressing the anticipated energy crisis and environmental issues [13–16]. However, there are still many challenges that must be addressed for practical application: namely, the high overpotential for CO2 activation, the low selectivity for the desired products, and the low stability of the electrocatalyst. Thus, an efficient catalyst is in high demand. The use of multicomponent materials is one promising route for designing Received March 19, 2019; accepted April 26, 2019 E-mail: tjuwanghua@tju.edu.cn
efficient catalysts [17–20]. Thus, metal/oxide bimetallic nanomaterials have aroused enormous interest. As reported, Cu-based electrocatalysts, especially copper oxides combined with active metals such as Au and Ag, exhibit improved catalytic behavior, distinct from that of the constituent elements [21–24]. In this context, we were inspired to fabricate a novel kind of Ag/Cu2O (Au/Cu2O) electrocatalyst for the ERC via a galvanic replacement strategy. Herein, Cu2O nanospheres are first synthesized in polyol-polyvinylpyrrolidone-cetyl trimethyl ammonium bromide (polyol-PVP-CTAB) solution. Thereafter, using Cu2O as a sacrificial template, a series of Ag/Cu2O composites is fabricated via a galvanic replacement reaction, in which a hierarchical nanostructured Ag/Cu2O composite is formed by varying the Ag/Cu atomic ratio. Through the same strategy, Au/Cu2O with a flower-like structure is also synthesized. Furthermore, these composites are applied in the ERC, and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) and electrolysis tests are used to evaluate the catalytic performance in terms of the current density, Faradaic efficiency (FE) of each product, and the stability. The higher electroactive surface area and combined electrocatalytic properties of Cu2O and Ag, as advantageous features, lead to the expectation of improved catalytic performance in the ERC. Thus, this study aims to develop a facile method of synthesizing a hierarchicalstructured noble metal-metal oxide composite as a highly efficient and stable electrocatalyst for the ERC.

sections.heading: 2 Materials and methods
sections.text:
All the reagents were used as received without any further purification. Cu(CH3COO)2 (98%) and HAuCl4 (99%) were purchased from HEOWNS (China), AgNO3 (99.8%) was purchased from Aladdin (China), polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP; MW = 58000) was purchased from Guangfu (China), cetyltrimethyl ammonium bromide (CTAB; 99%) was purchased from Kemiou Chemical Reagent (China), ethylene glycol (EG, AR) and acetone (AR, 99.8%) were purchased from Yuanli Chemical Reagent (China), and KHCO3 (99.5%) was purchased from J&K Scientific Limited (China).
2.1 Synthesis of Ag/Cu2O and Au/Cu2O composites
Firstly, Cu2O spheres were synthesized via a facile solvothermal method. The typical procedure is as follows: 40 mg PVP, 25 mg CTAB, and 50 mL EG were placed into a three-necked flask under constant magnetic stirring (300 r∙min–1) and heated in an oil bath. When the temperature reached 140°C, 9 mL of 0.11 mol∙L–1 Cu(CH3COO)2 solution was injected. The mixture was heated to 170°C and maintained for 10 min under continuous stirring. The color of the mixture solution changed from deep blue to
dark green, indicating the formation of Cu2O. After the solution cooled to room temperature, Cu2O was separated by centrifugation with acetone, pure water, and ethanol at 8000 r∙min–1 for 10 min in sequence. The obtained precipitates were dried at 60°C for 24 h in a vacuum oven. For the synthesis of Ag/Cu2O, the Cu2O spheres were not separated from the solution. In one pot, the required amount of AgNO3 solution was added to the Cu2Ocontaining mother solution at 170°C. The mixture was stirred for another 10 min, during which the color of the solution changed from dark green to deep gray. Finally, the suspension was centrifuged and the obtained solid was dried under the same conditions as mentioned above. The Ag content of the Ag/Cu2O composites was tuned by varying the concentration of the AgNO3 solution. The samples are denoted as Agx/Cu2O, where x represents the atomic ratio of Ag to Cu added to the reaction mixture. The obtained products are accordingly denoted as Ag0.125/ Cu2O, Ag0.25/Cu2O, Ag0.5/Cu2O, and Ag1/Cu2O. Galvanic replacement was also employed to synthesize Au/Cu2O using the as-prepared Cu2O nanospheres as a template. In the typical procedure: 7.2 mg of Cu2O nanospheres was added to 26 mL deionized water at room temperature. Thereafter, 3 mL PVP aqueous solution (1.0 wt-%) was added to the above solution under stirring, followed by 0.5 mL of 0.06 mol∙L–1 aqueous chloroauric acid solution. After 3 h of reaction, the suspension was centrifuged. The obtained solid was washed with pure water and ethanol, and dried at 60°C for 24 h in a vacuum oven.
2.2 Electrochemical measurements
All electrochemical measurements were carried out in a H-type two-compartment electrochemical cell separated by a proton exchange Nafion membrane. The catalyst ink consisted of 15 mg catalyst, 850 mL ethanol, and 150 mL Nafion. A glassy carbon electrode (GCE, 1.0 cm 1.0 cm) coated with catalyst ink was used as the working electrode. A platinum plate (1.0 cm 2.0 cm) was used as the counter-electrode, and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) served as the reference electrode. The applied potentials were converted to the potentials vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) according the reported equation (E(RHE) = E(SCE) + 0.0591 pH+ 0.24). All electrochemical measurements were carried out in 0.1 mol∙L–1 KHCO3 solution. In the LSV measurements, the potential scan was performed in the range of -0.1 to -1.4 V vs. RHE, and the system was purged with N2 and CO2 in sequence. The performance of the electrocatalysts in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 was analyzed by keeping the volume of the headspace in the cathode compartment at approximately 50 mL. The electrolyte was constantly purged with CO2 at a flow of 20 mL$min
–1 to keep the KHCO3 solution saturated with CO2. The catholyte was magnetically stirred to enhance the mass transport of CO2.
2 Front. Chem. Sci. Eng.
The gaseous products were assayed by gas chromatography and the liquid products were analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
2.3 Characterization
The morphologies of Cu2O and the Ag/Cu2O and Au/ Cu2O composites were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM, Japan, JEOLJ, EM2100F), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Japan, Hitachi Limited, S4800). Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD, Japan, Rigaku Corporation, D/MAX-2500) was employed to examine the composition and phase purity. The XRD data were acquired in the 2q range 25°-85° at a scanning speed of 6°∙min–1. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, America, PerkinElmer, PHI 1600) was employed to analyze the surface composition and chemical states of the samples. The electrochemical measurements were executed with a PGSTAT 302N (Switzerland, AutoLab Metrohm) instrument. The CO2 reduction gas-phase products were quantified by gas chromatography (America, Agilent, 7890B) with a thermal conductivity detector, and the liquid-phase products were quantified with a 700 MHz 1H/1D liquid NMR spectrometer (Switzerland, Bruker, AVANCE III).

sections.heading: 3 Results and discussion
sections.text:
3.1 Structure and morphology of Ag/Cu2O composites
As illustrated in Scheme 1, the Cu2O nanospheres were synthesized in EG-PVP-CTAB solution. The Ag/Cu2O composites were fabricated in one pot through galvanic replacement of the Cu+ ions with Ag+ ions via the following reactions: Cu2O+ 2H
+ ! 2Cu+ + H2O; Cu+ + Ag+ ! Cu2+ + Ag.
The Cu2O nanospheres were sacrificed to form Cu 2+ ions by gradual dissolution in the solution, accompanied by the growth of Ag on the etched Cu2O surfaces. Under specific conditions, silver tends to grow epitaxially to form nanoflakes that may aggregate and eventually form a hierarchical structure [25]. Figures 1(a) and (b) display the morphology of the asprepared Cu2O nanospheres. The SEM image exhibits large-scale uniform nanospheres with a narrow size distribution at about 180 nm, which is smaller than those in previous works [26–29]. Additionally, these Cu2O nanospheres consist of numerous stacking subunits, which are clearly indicated as close-packed slices in Fig. 1(b). This might be derived from the effect of PVP, which results in the formation of slices because PVP is preferentially adsorbed on Cu2O (111) and then induces growth along the (111) plane [29]. This is further evidenced by the interplanar spacing of 0.240 nm, assigned to Cu2O (111), in the inset HRTEM image. In the subsequent procedure, AgNO3 solution was directly added when the color of the solution changed from deep blue to dark green, which is an indicator of the formation of Cu2O. Agx/Cu2O composites were fabricated by changing the amount of Ag+ ions. Notably, assynthesized Ag0.125/Cu2O presents a unique morphology, as displayed in Figs. 1(c) and (d). The overall shape of the Cu2O nanosphere was maintained, but with a flower-like structure consisting of intersecting nanoflakes growing on an inner Cu2O sphere. The peripheral size increased to ~400 nm. Furthermore, the TEM image clearly reveals that the clusters of nanoflakes encompassed the core sphere, constructing a hierarchical flower-like structure. From the HRTEM image of the peripheral flake region, the fringe spacings were 0.231 nm and 0.205 nm, corresponding to the Ag (111) and Ag (200) planes, respectively. The elemental mapping in Fig. 1(e) also indicates dense distribution of the Cu and O atoms in the inner portion, whereas fewer Ag atoms were scattered throughout the
Scheme 1 Schematic illustration of synthesis of Cu2O and Ag/Cu2O composites.
Mengyun Wang et al. Nano-Ag(Au)/Cu2O as electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction 3
nanosphere. The above results suggest that the flower morphology of Ag0.125/Cu2O consists of Ag petals and a Cu2O core, indicating successful synthesis of the Agmodified Cu2O bimetallic nanostructure. When the amount of Ag+ was increased, the morphology varied significantly, as shown in Fig. 2. The images of Ag0.25/Cu2O in Figs. 2(a) and 2(d) reveal that only part of the nanospheres possessed the hierarchical flower-like structure, accompanied by a number of rigid spherical nanoparticles with rugged surfaces, which plausibly arise when the peripheral flakes become densely packed with the continuous formation of Ag. Furthermore, both Ag0.5/ Cu2O and Ag1/Cu2O were formed as irregular aggregates. As reported [25,30], Ag growth in the presence of organic acids tends to form flake-like structures that are loosely clustered into a flower-like structure. When the concentration of Ag+ is low, the rate of the galvanic replacement reaction between Cu+ and Ag+ is relatively slow, which facilitates epitaxial growth extending from the Cu2O sphere. The galvanic replacement reaction is accelerated in the presence of a large amount of Ag+. As a result, the original nanosphere structure of the Cu2O template gradually collapsed. Without the uniform template, the irregular shape would become dominant [25]. Moreover, epitaxial growth tends to be suppressed as the concentration of H+ decreases due to consumption in the galvanic replacement reaction. The composition and phase purity of the as-prepared samples were characterized by XRD. Figure 3 shows diffraction peaks at 36.41°, 42.30°, 61.34°, and 73.53°, indexed to the standard Cu2O diffractions of the (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes, respectively
4 Front. Chem. Sci. Eng.
(PDF#04-0836). For the Agx/Cu2O samples, new, sharp peaks appeared at 38.26°, 44.47°, 64.71°, 77.73° and 81.90°, indicating the formation of face-centered cubic crystalline Ag (PDF#04-0783). Moreover, as the amount of Ag+ ions increased, the intensities of the Ag crystal peaks became stronger, while the Cu2O diffraction peaks
became less intense. Notably, the Cu2O peaks could not be observed in the XRD spectra of Ag0.5/Cu2O and Ag1/ Cu2O. Overall, the obtained XRD patterns indicate the coexistence of Ag and Cu2O in the as-prepared Ag/Cu2O samples. Diffraction peaks assigned to C in the carbon support used to load the samples were also detected. Furthermore, to investigate the surface composition and chemical states of the Agx/Cu2O composites, XPS analysis was performed, as shown in Fig. 4 and Figs. S1-S4 (cf. Electronic Supplementary Material, ESM). Figure 4(a) shows the XPS survey spectrum of Ag0.125/Cu2O, indicating that it consisted of Cu, Ag, and O. The Ag 3d levels of Ag0.125/Cu2O show two peaks at 367.8 and 373.8 eV, assigned to the 3d5/2 and Ag 3d3/2 states, respectively, which shifted to lower binding energies than those of pure silver (368.2 and 374.2 eV) due to the electronic interaction between Ag and Cu2O [24]. Furthermore, the profile of the Cu2O sample (Fig. S1, cf. ESM) shows two Cu 2p peaks at 953.1 eV and 932.3 eV, indicating the presence of the Cu(I) oxidation state. In contrast, the profiles of Ag0.125/Cu2O and the other samples with Ag (Fig. S2-S4, cf. ESM) exhibit two other Cu 2p peaks at ~933.5 and ~942.1 eV, which are assigned to Cu(II) species. This might result from electron transfer from Cu2O to Ag due to the difference in the electronic environment or the generation of small amounts of undissolved Cu2+ ions during the galvanic replacement
Mengyun Wang et al. Nano-Ag(Au)/Cu2O as electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction 5
reaction [24,31–33]. The O 1s spectra in Fig. 4(d) display a broad and asymmetric peak, which could be resolved into two peaks at 530.1 and 531.6 eV, attributed to the oxygen in the oxides and the adsorbed oxygen, respectively [12]. Based on the quantitative XPS data, the elemental contents are summarized in Table S1, demonstrating that the atomic ratio of Ag to Cu increased with increasing addition of AgNO3, consistent with the XRD results.
3.2 Electrochemical measurements of Agx/Cu2O composites
3.2.1 LSV measurements
LSV measurements of the Cu2O and Agx/Cu2O composites were performed between -0.1 and -1.4 V vs. RHE in aqueous 0.1 mol∙L–1 KHCO3 electrolyte at a potential scan rate of 50 mV$s–1. The optimum catalyst loading was determined as 1.5 mg$cm–2. The LSV curves are shown in Figs. 5(a-e). The black dashed line and red solid line represent the LSV curves obtained in N2 saturated and CO2 saturated 0.1 mol∙L–1 KHCO3 solution, respectively. The discrepancy in the current determined from the black and red lines is used to determine the partial current density related to CO2 reduction, as shown in Fig. 5(f). The larger current discrepancy indicates better electrocatalytic activity for CO2 reduction. Compared with Cu2O, the Ag/Cu2O catalysts all demonstrate enhanced electroactivity for CO2 reduction. The most significant improvement was obtained with Ag0.125/Cu2O. This may be attributed to its unique hierarchical structure, which provides a large surface area. Furthermore, to evaluate the stability, Cu2O,
6 Front. Chem. Sci. Eng.
Ag0.125/Cu2O, and Ag0.25/Cu2O used in the 1 h electrolysis process were again subjected to the LSV test. The results are represented by blue dashed lines in Figs. 5(a-c). Similar to a prior observation, used Cu2O displayed a much larger current density at high potential (> -0.7 V) than as-prepared Cu2O, which might be ascribed to formation of the more conductive Cu due to the deep reduction of Cu2O during the 1-h electrocatalysis process. In contrast, the Agx/Cu2O composites presented better stability, as evidenced by the overlap of the red and blue lines. Therefore, the reduction of Cu2O was significantly inhibited by the introduction of peripheral clusters of Ag nanoflakes, and the stability was thus maintained.
3.2.2 Electroactive surface area (ESA) measurements
The relative magnitude of the ESA of Cu2O and Agx/Cu2O was compared based on the electrochemical capacitance in the double layer region, because the electrochemical activity is related to the structure and ESA. Generally, the capacitive current in the potential range in which the Faraday reaction does not occur is determined by cyclic voltammetry at various scanning rates. Herein, the positive and negative capacitive currents at the center of the potential window were determined by potentiostatic cycling in the range of -0.21 to -0.43 V at scan rates from 20 to 100 mV$s–1 and averaged and plotted against the scan rate to obtain the capacitance, as shown in Figs. S5 and S6 (cf. ESM). Among these samples, Ag0.125/Cu2O displayed the highest double-layer capacitance of 3.62 mF. Because the double-layer capacitance is proportional to the ESA, it is deduced that Ag0.125/Cu2O possesses the largest ESA among these samples, and in turn more active sites should be present on Ag0.125/Cu2O, resulting in the excellent performance in the ERC, in agreement with the above LSV data.
3.2.3 Product distribution from electrochemical reduction of CO2
To demonstrate the product distribution from the ECR using the Cu2O and Agx/Cu2O samples, electrolysis experiments were conducted for 5 h in CO2-saturated 0.1 mol∙L–1 KHCO3 solution at the specific potentials. The products were analyzed and the corresponding FE was calculated. The results are illustrated in Figs. 6(a–e). The detected gaseous products are identified as H2 and CO, and the only detected liquid product was identified as HCOOH. Comparison of the product distribution of Cu2O with that of Agx/Cu2O revealed that the combination of Ag with Cu2O nanospheres greatly facilitated the reduction of CO2, rather than the dominant formation of H2 in the case of Cu2O. It is also noteworthy that the Agx/Cu2O catalysts all favored the formation of CO via CO2 reduction, instead of HCOOH that was generated on Cu2O, as evidenced by the
lower FEHCOOH and much higher FECO than those of Cu2O. Plausibly due to the trace amount of Ag in the Agx/ Cu2O catalysts, there was no significant increase in FECO, although the Ag content increased. Importantly, considering Ag as a noble active component, it was found that Ag0.125/Cu2O exhibited the highest CO evolution rate per microgram of Ag during electrolysis over the course of 5 h, followed by Ag0.25/Cu2O (Fig. 6(f)). This may be associated with the hierarchical flower-like structures, which could provide a larger ESA [5,12]. As shown in Figs. S5 and S6 (cf. ESM), Ag0.125/Cu2O displayed the highest ESA of 3.62 mF. The striking difference in the current density and FE profiles of the Agx/Cu2O samples and Cu2O also confirms the enhanced selectivity for CO via CO2 reduction and better stability due to the modification with Ag, as shown in Fig. 7. The morphologies of the used Cu2O and Ag0.125/Cu2O samples were characterized by SEM. As displayed in Fig. S7 (cf. ESM), the overall morphology of the used Cu2O nanosphere changed significantly. Aggregates comprising numerous irregular particles were observed, instead of the asprepared uniform nanospheres. In contrast, the used Ag0.125/Cu2O maintained the flower-like structure with up-right nanoflakes, indicative of its excellent stability.
3.3 Au/Cu2O composite and its catalytic performance in CO2 reduction
Through the same strategy, we successfully prepared the Au0.6/Cu2O composite with a hierarchical flower-like structure, as shown in Fig. 8(a). In contrast with Ag0.125/ Cu2O, the nanoflakes were thick and densely packed. The XRD pattern in Fig. 8(b) shows diffraction peaks at 38.18°, 44.39°, 64.58°, 64.58°, 77.55° and 81.72°, assigned to the (111), (200), (220), (311) and (222) crystal planes of Au (PDE#04-0784), indicating the successful introduction of Au [24]. The diffraction peaks of Cu2O might be shielded due to the strong peaks of Au. Similar to Ag0.125/Cu2O, the ESA of Au0.6/Cu2O was higher than that of the Cu2O nanospheres, as indicated by the double-layer capacitance of 2.68 mF (Fig. S6, cf. ESM). Remarkably, the Au0.6/ Cu2O composite also exhibited better CO2 reduction activity than the Cu2O nanospheres, as evidenced by the partial current of CO2 reduction shown in Fig. 8(c). The product distribution obtained with Au0.6/Cu2O (Fig. 8(d)) demonstrates that the FECO of this sample was ~10% higher than that of Ag0.125/Cu2O and the former also exhibits excellent stability.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, novel hierarchical flower-like Ag/Cu2O and Au/Cu2O nanostructured composites were synthesized via a facile galvanic replacement reaction. The composites exhibit efficient electrocatalytic performance in the
Mengyun Wang et al. Nano-Ag(Au)/Cu2O as electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction 7
electrochemical reduction of CO2. First, Cu2O nanospheres, with a uniform particle size of ~180 nm, were prepared. Thereafter, Ag/Cu2O composites were fabricated by using Cu2O as a sacrificial template. By varying the Ag/ Cu atomic ratio, a Ag0.125/Cu2O composite possessing a hierarchical flower-like nanostructure with intersecting Ag nanoflakes encompassing an inner Cu2O sphere were prepared. The catalytic performance in the ERC was evaluated in terms of the FE of each product and current density. In comparison with the Cu2O nanospheres, the Ag/ Cu2O samples all present a higher FECO and somewhat suppressed H2 evolution due to the combination of the catalytic ability of Ag combined with Cu2O. Notably, Ag0.125/Cu2O exhibited the highest CO evolution rate as a result of the hierarchical structure, which provides a larger electroactive surface area. The obtained Au0.6/Cu2O composite with the same flower-like structure presented superior catalytic performance with a 10% higher FECO. Importantly, the results reveal that Ag0.125/Cu2O and Au0.6/Cu2O exhibit remarkably improved stability over that of Cu2O. This study presents a facile way to synthesize hierarchical noble metal-metal oxide composites for designing highly efficient and stable electrocatalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2.
